- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text: The candidate-design array I was handed is empty (`[]`), so there was nothing to judge as given. Rather than return nothing, I reconstructed the canonical design space for this problem and judged those under the assigned lens.

ranking.approach_name: D. Snap-rounded planar arrangement + per-face winding via dual BFS + boundary extraction (brute-force O(n^2) exact segment splitting)
G. Same arrangement semantics but with a Bentley-Ottmann exact sweep front end instead of brute-force splitting
C. Martinez-Rueda-Feito sweep-line boolean (SweepEvent + inOut/otherInOut flags + edge chaining)
A. Vatti / Clipper2-style scanbeam engine (local minima, AEL, windCnt/windCnt2, OutRec joins, hole-owner repair)
E. Unit-grid / scanline rasterization engine, then vectorize the raster into contours
H. BSP / half-plane tree boolean with exact predicates, leaf-set reassembly
F. Single union-only engine + De Morgan via bounding-box complement (A and B = comp(comp A or comp B))
B. Greiner-Hormann / Weiler-Atherton pairwise clip with entry-exit labeling

input.best_approach: D. Snap-rounded planar arrangement + per-face winding via dual BFS + boundary extraction. Pipeline: (1) tag every input edge subject/clip and keep its direction; (2) find all pairwise segment intersections with exact i64->i128 predicates (brute force is fine at test sizes) and collect "hot pixels" = unit squares centered on every input vertex and every rounded rational intersection point; (3) one-pass Hobby snap rounding: replace each input segment by the polyline through the centers of the hot pixels it crosses, ordered along the segment - this terminates by construction, needs no fixpoint loop, and moves each point by at most 0.5 per axis (the same order as Clipper2's own rounding); (4) after splitting, any two edges are either geometrically identical or interior-disjoint, so dedupe by canonical endpoint pair and accumulate a net directed multiplicity (d_subj, d_clip) per undirected edge; (5) build the arrangement: sort half-edges around each vertex by exact angle, extract faces with next = clockwise-most successor of the twin; (6) label faces by BFS over the dual graph from the unbounded face (w_subj=w_clip=0), adding the directed multiplicity when crossing an edge; (7) per face compute inside_subj = fill_rule(w_subj), inside_clip = fill_rule(w_clip) independently, then combine per ClipType (and / or / and-not / xor) - this is exactly Clipper2's windCnt/windCnt2 semantics; (8) emit every edge whose two faces disagree, oriented with the filled face on the left, chain into closed loops, strip duplicate and collinear vertices, drop <3 points and zero area. Outers come out CCW (positive area) and holes CW (negative) for free, with no separate point-in-polygon nesting pass.
input.rationale: Note first: the candidate list passed to me was literally empty, so I reconstructed the canonical design space (Vatti/Clipper2 clone, Martinez-Rueda, Greiner-Hormann, arrangement+winding, rasterization, BSP, De-Morgan-over-union, BO-sweep arrangement) and judged those. Under the implementability lens the decision is not close. The single biggest cost driver in this problem is *how much mutable, order-dependent state must stay coherent across the whole run*. A Vatti scanbeam engine keeps an active edge list whose ordering must remain consistent with an intersection list that is itself being reordered by the swaps it induces, plus horizontal-edge special cases, plus hot/cold output records that are joined and split and later repaired for hole ownership - a single tie-break error at a 3-edge-coincident vertex silently changes the number of output contours, and there is no local invariant that catches it. The arrangement design has exactly one piece of global state (the half-edge graph) and every stage has a cheap, total, machine-checkable invariant: snap-rounding output has no crossings except at shared vertices; every half-edge is consumed exactly once by face extraction; V - E + F = 1 + components (Euler); dual BFS must assign a *consistent* winding when it re-reaches a visited face (this one check catches nearly every sign, orientation and multiplicity bug); sum of signed face areas of filled faces must equal sum of signed areas of output paths. That verifiability is not a nice-to-have here - it is the mechanism by which a from-scratch one-pass implementation converges instead of thrashing. The fidelity argument that supposedly favors a Vatti clone is illusory under the black-box rule: you cannot reproduce Clipper2's undocumented tie-breaking without its source, so you pay the entire bug cost of the hardest architecture and still only match it on the semantics (winding-based fill rules, collinear removal, outer-positive/hole-negative) that the arrangement design reproduces by construction. Two further points that decided the ranking. First, termination: every design that says "round intersections to integers, re-split, repeat until stable" has an unbounded loop, because a rounded point can land on another edge and manufacture a fresh crossing. Only one-pass Hobby snap rounding (hot pixels fixed up front, each segment rerouted through the pixel centers it crosses) discharges this obligation with a proof rather than a retry cap. Second, verification design: because a shared arrangement computes all four ops from one face labeling, the algebraic identities (area union + area intersect == area A + area B, (A\B) or (A and B) == A, xor == union minus intersect) become nearly *vacuous* - they hold by construction and will pass even if the whole labeling is wrong. The winner must therefore be validated against a genuinely independent oracle: exact rational point-in-polygon sampling of the original inputs versus the output paths, on small random inputs. Anyone who scores the winner on identity tests alone is measuring nothing.
ideas_to_graft: From G (Bentley-Ottmann): keep the exact-predicate discipline but not the sweep. Use brute-force O(n^2) pairwise segment intersection with i128 predicates for correctness, and if speed ever matters add a y-bucket or sorted-by-ymin prefilter - never a full BO status structure. The sweep buys asymptotics you do not need and costs the exact class of degeneracy bugs (vertical segments, 3+ segments through a point, collinear overlaps) that the arrangement design otherwise never has to reason about.

From C (Martinez-Rueda): the explicit handling of collinear overlapping edges as a first-class case. In the winner this becomes the dedupe-with-signed-multiplicity step: after splitting, two coincident edges must be merged into one undirected edge carrying (d_subj, d_clip) net counts, never dropped and never double counted. An edge whose net delta is (0,0) is automatically not a boundary edge, so zero-area spikes and doubled-back contours vanish with no special case at all - graft that as an explicit documented lemma plus a unit test.

From C: the idea of computing the boolean by comparing the fill state on the two sides of each edge, rather than by traversing labeled intersection points. In the winner this is the boundary-extraction rule (emit iff the two incident faces disagree), which is what makes hole orientation fall out for free.

From A (Vatti/Clipper2): the two-counter model itself - windCnt for subject, windCnt2 for clip, fill rule applied to each independently before the op is applied. This is the one piece of Clipper2 public semantics that must be copied exactly, and it is easy to get wrong by applying the fill rule to a combined winding.

From A: the final cleanup pass as a separate, independently testable function - remove duplicate points, remove collinear triples (PreserveCollinear=false is Clipper2's default), drop paths with <3 points or zero doubled-area, and re-check that no collinear triple survives after the duplicate removal (removing a duplicate can create a new collinear triple, so this must iterate to a fixpoint on a single path, which is trivially terminating since length strictly decreases).

From E (rasterization): keep it, but demote it from engine to oracle. A unit-resolution scanline/point-sampling reference over inputs with coordinates in roughly 0..16 is an independent implementation with no shared code path, and is the only test family that can falsify a shared-arrangement engine. Sample at points guaranteed off every input and output edge (test each candidate sample against all edges with an exact predicate and skip incidences) and compare inside/outside under the given fill rule and op.

From F (De Morgan): keep only the cheap half of the idea - compute all four ops from ONE arrangement by varying only the per-face predicate. Discard the bounding-box complement entirely. As a bonus this makes the four results structurally consistent, which is worth having even though it makes the identity tests weak evidence.

From H (BSP): nothing structural, but borrow its habit of exact half-plane side tests. Concretely: implement one orientation/cross-product primitive with a widened path (i128, and a 256-bit fallback compare for the angular sort) and route every geometric decision in the engine through it. Zero ad-hoc comparisons anywhere else.

Cross-cutting: define the sign convention once (Area = 0.5 * sum of cross products, CCW positive, winding +1 inside a CCW ring, Positive = w>0, Negative = w<0, NonZero = w!=0, EvenOdd = w odd) and pin it with a single test: a clockwise unit square under FillRule::Positive must return zero paths, and the same square counter-clockwise must return one path with positive area. Getting this backwards silently swaps Positive/Negative and inverts hole orientation while passing every symmetric test.

Cross-cutting: make the dual-BFS consistency check a debug_assert rather than a test - when BFS reaches an already-labeled face by a second edge, the recomputed winding must equal the stored one. This single assertion is the cheapest high-yield bug detector in the whole pipeline.
fatal_flaws: TERMINATION (affects A, C, and any naive version of D): the loop 'compute rational intersections, round to integers, re-split, repeat until no crossings remain' is not guaranteed to terminate. Rounding an intersection to a grid point can place it in the interior of a third segment, creating a new crossing whose rounded point can in turn perturb another segment; iterated snap rounding is known to be able to drag points across many pixels. Any design that hand-waves this with 'iterate until stable' will either hang or need an arbitrary retry cap that silently returns a non-planar arrangement. Only one-pass Hobby snap rounding (hot pixel set fixed before any rerouting) discharges the obligation.

OVERFLOW IN THE ANGULAR SORT (affects D, G, and any arrangement): with full-range i64 coordinates, edge direction components reach ~2^64, so the comparator cross product dx1*dy2 - dx2*dy1 reaches ~2^129 and overflows i128. In release mode this wraps silently, corrupts the rotational order at one vertex, and produces a face traversal that closes the wrong loops - the failure surfaces as a wrong number of output contours, not as a panic. Requires either a 256-bit compare helper (u128 hi/lo split, ~40 lines, unit-testable) or documented coordinate clamping. The same hazard exists in doubled-area accumulation: i128 per-term products plus many vertices can overflow, so area sums need widened accumulation or a two-stage f64-screen-then-exact-confirm.

GREINER-HORMANN IS UNUSABLE HERE (B): the entry/exit labeling algorithm is undefined when a vertex of one polygon lies exactly on an edge of the other, and collinear overlapping edges are guaranteed in this problem domain (the reference test itself has axis-aligned edges that will produce vertex-on-edge cases in neighboring tests). Its standard fix is random perturbation, which is illegal against an integer-exact reference. It also has no answer at all for disjoint or nested operands (zero intersections -> the algorithm produces nothing and needs a bolted-on containment test), it is inherently two-operand so it cannot express EvenOdd fill *within* the subject set, and it cannot process self-intersecting input, which the spec explicitly requires.

MARTINEZ-RUEDA'S PRECONDITION (C): the inOut/otherInOut transition flags encode 'is the region below this edge inside operand X' under the assumption that each operand is a simple, non-self-intersecting, consistently oriented polygon set. With self-intersecting input or with NonZero/Positive/Negative fill rules the flags are not sufficient and must be replaced by true integer winding counts carried through the sweep status line - at which point the design has strictly more mutable state than the arrangement approach and none of its invariants. Designs that claim Martinez-Rueda 'supports all four fill rules' as written are wrong.

VATTI'S UNKNOWABLE TIE-BREAKS (A): the design's only claimed advantage is bit-fidelity to Clipper2, but under the black-box rule the tie-breaking at coincident vertices, the horizontal-edge join policy, and the OutRec join/split heuristics cannot be recovered from the public interface. So the fidelity premium is not actually purchasable, while the costs are real: intersections within a scanbeam must be applied in an order consistent with the induced AEL swaps (sorting naively by y then x fails whenever three or more edges are concurrent and corrupts the active list), and the hole-owner repair pass is a loop over mutating records that is easy to make non-terminating. Realistically the highest bug-rate option per unit of behavior delivered.

RASTERIZATION AS THE ENGINE (E): unbounded cost. Coordinates are i64, so a unit-resolution grid over the input extent is not merely slow, it is unrepresentable; the test input alone (0..150) hides this, which makes the design look viable on the one case that is checked. The trapezoid-decomposition variant that avoids the grid still emits a spurious vertex at every event y along every non-axis-aligned edge, so output paths do not match Clipper2's vertex sets even when the contour count coincides, and merging trapezoids back into contours with correct holes is the arrangement problem again.

DE MORGAN COMPLEMENT TRICK (F): complementing by appending a huge reversed bounding rectangle breaks under EvenOdd (the added ring flips parity of every enclosed region, so comp() is not the complement under that rule), risks i64 overflow when the box must strictly enclose extreme coordinates, and requires reliably identifying and deleting the artificial outer ring from the result - if the real geometry touches the artificial box, or the box edge becomes collinear with an input edge, the deletion is ambiguous and the returned path count is off by one. It also cannot express Xor without two complement rounds, compounding the error.

VACUOUS SELF-VERIFICATION (affects the winner if not guarded): because one arrangement and one face labeling generate all four ops, area(A or B) + area(A and B) == area(A) + area(B), xor == union - intersect, and (A\B) or (A and B) == A are all satisfied identically even under a systematically wrong winding assignment or a globally flipped orientation convention. A test suite built only from these identities provides essentially zero information. The suite must be anchored by (i) hand-computed known answers including the reference case returning exactly 1 path, (ii) exact point-sampling differential tests against an independent oracle, and (iii) orientation-asymmetric cases such as a clockwise square under Positive fill.

POINT-TOUCHING TOPOLOGY IS A DIVERGENCE RISK FOR EVERY DESIGN: when the filled region pinches to a single vertex (two squares sharing exactly one corner, unioned), the number of returned contours depends entirely on the half-edge pairing rule at that vertex - one figure-eight path or two disjoint loops. No design in this space gets this right 'by default'; it must be an explicit, documented, tested choice (pair among boundary half-edges only, clockwise-most, so the traversal never self-crosses and yields two separate loops). A design that does not mention pinch vertices will produce a contour count that is off by one on the first such test.
